projects.title: Which Employers Reliably Sponsor H-1B Business Roles
projects.hook: SQL analysis of 3.47M H-1B filings (2020–2023). The business-role wage premium survives on medians — then breaks honestly when IT managers are excluded.
projects.visualAlt: Wage premium by year, business vs data roles

body.problem: International graduates pick a track first and ask about visa risk later — on anecdote. Nobody could say whether business and analytics tracks differ on approval odds, or which employers sponsor every year rather than once.
body.approach: Normalized 3.47M federal filings into a five-table MySQL database, then ran eight queries on volume, approval, pay, and four-year employer durability.
body.hers: Reported the median that broke my own headline finding — the premium flips when IT managers are excluded.
body.result: Approval gap never passed 1.7 points. Business volume +9.1% while analytics fell 6.1%. 77 durable business sponsors identified — EY leads with 13,329 filings at 97.8%.
body.lesson: Visa risk is the wrong variable. The decision turns on market direction and pay, not approval odds.

projects.setting: Solo, in two stages. Python for Massachusetts, then SQL for the whole country.
projects.context: International graduates choose between business and analytics roles partly on which gets sponsored. The advice they get is anecdote.
projects.outcome: Across 3,471,247 filings, approval rates never differed by more than 1.7 points.
calls: Kept every duplicate: dropping them would have flipped the ranking.
Reported medians. One hourly-keyed salary turned $195,870 into $407 million.

projects.title: Massachusetts H-1B Analysis
projects.hook: Reading the Massachusetts labor market through five years of public H-1B filing data: which employers sponsor repeatedly, and do business roles pay as well as analytics roles?
projects.visualAlt: Median pay: business roles vs data-and-analytics roles
projects.diagramAlt: Trap, Insight, Machine: the build-post framework

body.problem: I'm on an F-1 visa. The job search isn't just finding the right role — it's finding an employer who'll go the full distance: OPT to STEM OPT to H-1B. I needed to know whether the business roles I'd apply to get sponsored as often, and pay as well, as the data-and-analytics roles.
body.approach: Filtered 137,866 Massachusetts H-1B filings (FY2020-2024) to 123,497 certified, normalized every wage to annual, grouped roles by federal occupation code instead of keywords, and compared business vs analytics with bootstrap confidence intervals on the medians.
body.hers: Caught 2,583 IT managers hiding in the business group through their occupation code — they'd inflated the business median to $115,000. Re-ran without them: $105,000. The notebook shows exactly what changed.
body.result: 13,672 business filings vs 14,035 analytics. $105,000 vs $104,000 median pay — statistically the same. 0% vs 100% STEM — the H-1B clock is tighter on the business side.
body.lesson: Pay doesn't decide the track — the visa clock does. Same money, different runway.

projects.setting: Solo. Python, pandas, matplotlib — one notebook, 22 cells, reproducible end to end.
projects.context: International graduates choose between business and analytics roles partly on which gets sponsored — and whether the pay justifies the track.
projects.outcome: Business roles pay effectively the same as analytics roles: $105,000 vs $104,000 median. The difference is the visa clock — 0% STEM vs 100% STEM.
calls: Kept 32,867 exact duplicates: a repeated filing is an employer sponsoring again.
Reported medians, not means — typo'd pay units turned one $195,870 salary into $407 million.
Grouped by federal occupation code, then pulled 2,583 IT managers back out of the business group.

projects.title: Where Should We Spend the Next Ad Dollar?
projects.hook: A marketing analytics lead has an ad budget and a room full of managers who read the business through sales volume. This dashboard makes the case for spending it elsewhere, and lets the room test the recommendation live.

body.problem: Budget follows sales volume. Phones sells $330K, Chairs $328K, Tables is #4. So the money goes to the biggest sellers, including one that loses $17,725.
body.approach: Four linked views: sales bar, sales-vs-profit scatter, discount ladder, state map. A five-point Tableau Story walks the argument from what sells to Fund / Fix / Stop.
body.result: Fund Paper, Copiers, Accessories, Labels, Envelopes. Fix pricing first on Binders, Storage, Chairs. Stop funding Tables, Bookcases, Machines, Supplies. Capping discounts at 20% lifts profit 47% on its own.

calls: No discount level above 20% makes money: at or below 20% the business earns +$422K, above 20% it loses −$135K. The states confirm it independently: average discount and margin correlate at r = −0.98.

projects.title: Delivery Economics
projects.hook: A white-glove delivery operation losing $1,156 on 13 orders. I rebuilt the whole case from 171 raw order lines: the cost model, the 7-day operating schedule, and the operating system that runs the day.

body.problem: The flat-rate promise is a brand differentiator and a money loser: one customer pays $399 for 276 cubic feet, another pays $399 for 3,970.
body.approach: Geographic clustering, bin-pack to the 1,700 cu ft truck without splitting orders, assign to days inside the 540-minute window. Three alternatives tested: two trucks (+$1,092, rejected), luxury pace (+$3,040), bigger truck (−$1,664, the only lever that wins).
body.result: $6,043 cost vs $4,887 revenue: −$1,156, −23.7% margin. Eight of thirteen customers lose money. Volume-based pricing at $150 + $0.25/cu ft, and the bigger truck flips the loss into a $508 profit.

projects.context: 171 order lines, a 45-SKU item master, and customer addresses for zone mapping.
calls: The audit caught three contradictions in my own original files. All fixed from the primary sources. The loss moved from $808 to $1,156 and the thesis held.

projects.title: The Bounce-Back
projects.hook: A marketing performance audit that pulled a team out of a Q3 collapse and back to profitability by Q6.

body.problem: Our team launched an international bike company, placed second after Q1, then collapsed in Q3: zero paid search, 78% of orders unfulfilled, fragmented messaging, and the quarter's worst loss (-$360K operating profit).
body.approach: A diagnostic audit: benchmark every marketing dimension against the market, decompose losses by segment, trace each failure to an organizational root cause, then size a corrective plan with targets.
body.result: Operating profit went from -$360K (Q3) to nearly breakeven in Q4 (-$20K) to +$703K in Q6. Revenue grew 13x off the Q3 trough.

projects.context: Built from six quarters of a Harvard Business Publishing venture strategy simulation, where I served as VP of Business Analytics and HR.
calls: One honest complication: Q5 shows a -$717K loss. That's not a relapse. It's a deliberate $860K R&D investment while revenue kept climbing.
The turnaround is a profit story inside a share-loss market, which is the more interesting finding and the one a hiring manager can actually interrogate.
